resources.string: The words in quotes are Android\'s own names. Your phone may name them differently.
Android did not let Datapavan start its VPN. If the \"%1$s\" switch is on for another VPN app, turn it off first.
This phone\'s \"%2$s\" setting points to %1$s. Android sends the names that apps look up there, encrypted. This keeps them private from your network, but Datapavan cannot read them.

This phone\'s \"%3$s\" setting points to %1$s. Android then sends the names that apps look up to %1$s itself, encrypted, past Datapavan and past %2$s. Your network cannot read those names, but it can see that this phone uses %1$s. And %1$s sees the names and your real address on the internet. For the apps you send through %2$s, change the \"%3$s\" setting to \"%4$s\" or \"%5$s\".
Look for the \"%1$s\" setting in the settings that open. On some phones it is one step further in.
Android\'s \"%2$s\" setting sends every app\'s names to %1$s, past Datapavan. Your choice here applies only while that setting is \"%3$s\" or \"%4$s\".

Strict does not cover everything. Android checks the connection by itself, past Datapavan. Some apps use their own encrypted DNS. The apps you left out are not covered. And while Datapavan restarts its VPN, or if Android stops it while its \"%1$s\" switch is off, apps use the network\'s resolver.
Datapavan looks up this name through your network before the tunnel starts. If the \"%1$s\" setting is off, your network may see it.
This phone has no PIN, pattern or password set under the \"%1$s\" setting, so records of earlier days can be opened at any time. With one, they open only while the phone is unlocked.
